{
  "analysis": "The training data reveals that German legal texts contain person names in two primary contexts: judges/lawyers (preceded by titles like Dr., Mag., Prof., Univ.-Prof., Hon.-Prof., DI, Ing., Bakk. iur., etc.) and parties (preceded by context like 'klagenden Partei', 'beklagte Partei', 'Antragsteller', 'Angeklagten', or appearing at the start of a sentence). The main challenge is distinguishing these from capitalized nouns and ensuring titles are included in the match.",
  "strategy": "Use two focused regex rules: one for titles followed by names (covering judges/lawyers) and one for names appearing after specific legal role indicators or at sentence starts, ensuring high precision by anchoring to context.",
  "note": "Every rule includes output_template and output_key. Patterns use capture groups to extract the full name including titles where appropriate.",
  "rules": [
    {
      "name": "title_based_person",
      "description": "Matches person names preceded by common German legal/academic titles (Dr., Mag., Prof., DI, Ing., etc.)",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Senatspr\u00e4sident(?:in|en)?|Vizepr\u00e4sident(?:in)?|Hofrat(?:in)?|Richter(?:in)?|Anwalt(?:in)?|Rechtsanwalt(?:in)?|Generalprokurator(?:in)?|Schriftf\u00fchrer(?:in)?|Antragsgegner(?:in)?|Kl\u00e4ger(?:in)?|Beklagte(?:r)?|Antragsteller(?:in)?|Angeklagte(?:r)?|Staatsanwalt(?:in)?|Gesch\u00e4ftsf\u00fchrer(?:in)?|Vater|Mutter|Elternteil|Eltern)\b.*?(?:Dr\\.\\s+|Mag\\.\\s+|Univ\\.-Prof\\.\\s+|Hon\\.-Prof\\.\\s+|Prof\\.\\s+|DI\\.\\s+|Ing\\.\\s+|Bakk\\.\\s+iur\\.\\s+|PhD\\s+)([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+(?:MBA|MSc|BSc|LLM)?)?)(?:\\s+(?:und|oder)\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)?",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 10,
      "reasoning": "Captures names with titles following role indicators. The pattern handles complex titles and multiple names joined by 'und'."
    },
    {
      "name": "role_context_person",
      "description": "Matches person names appearing after specific legal role phrases without explicit titles, or at sentence start",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:der\\s+klagenden\\s+Partei\\s+|der\\s+beklagten\\s+Partei\\s+|der\\s+Antragsteller(?:in)?\\s+|der\\s+Antragsgegner(?:in)?\\s+|der\\s+Angeklagte(?:r)?\\s+|der\\s+Staatsanwaltschaft\\s+|gegen\\s+|vertreten\\s+durch\\s+(?:[A-Z][a-z]+\\s+)*)([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+(?:MBA|MSc|BSc|LLM)?)?)(?:\\s+(?:und|oder)\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)?",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 9,
      "reasoning": "Captures names in party roles where titles might be omitted or where the name follows a preposition like 'gegen' or 'vertreten durch'."
    },
    {
      "name": "sentence_start_person",
      "description": "Matches person names at the beginning of a sentence or after specific punctuation indicating a new entity",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:^|[.!?]\\s+)([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+(?:MBA|MSc|BSc|LLM)?)?)(?:\\s+(?:und|oder)\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)?",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 8,
      "reasoning": "Catches names at sentence starts which often appear in legal texts as party names or defendants."
    },
    {
      "name": "title_only_person",
      "description": "Matches names that start with a title but have no preceding role context (common for judges)",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?<![^A-Za-z])(Dr\\.\\s+|Mag\\.\\s+|Univ\\.-Prof\\.\\s+|Hon\\.-Prof\\.\\s+|Prof\\.\\s+|DI\\.\\s+|Ing\\.\\s+|Bakk\\.\\s+iur\\.\\s+|PhD\\s+)([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+(?:MBA|MSc|BSc|LLM)?)?)(?:\\s+(?:und|oder)\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)?",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1$2",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 7,
      "reasoning": "Handles cases where a title appears without a preceding role indicator, ensuring the full title+name is captured."
    }
  ],
  "deleted_rules": []
}

{
  "analysis": "The current rules fail because they match titles (Dr., Mag.) as separate entities or miss them entirely, and they incorrectly match sentence headers like 'Kopf Der Oberste Gerichtshof' due to overly broad sentence-start patterns. The 'role_context_person' rule is too greedy, capturing role titles like 'Rechtsanw' instead of names. The 'title_only_person' rule is missing the title in the output capture group.",
  "strategy": "1. Delete 'sentence_start_person' and 'role_context_person' as they are the primary sources of false positives. 2. Add a robust 'title_person' rule that captures the full title + name sequence (e.g., 'Dr. Name') using a negative lookbehind to avoid partial matches. 3. Add a 'role_context_name' rule that specifically looks for names following legal role phrases, ensuring the name starts with a capital letter and is not a title itself.",
  "rules": [
    {
      "name": "title_person",
      "description": "Matches person names preceded by German legal/academic titles (Dr., Mag., Prof., etc.) ensuring the full title+name is captured.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?<![A-Za-z])(?:(?:Hon\\.-?Prof\\.|Univ\\.-?Prof\\.|Prof\\.|Dr\\.|Mag\\.|DI\\.|Ing\\.|Bakk\\.\\s+iur\\.|PhD\\.|MMag\\.|HR\\s+Ing\\.|Techn\\s+|Dipl\\.-?HTL\\-?Ing\\.)\\s+)?([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+(?:LL\\.M\\.|MBA|MSc|BSc|PhD)?)?)(?:\\s+(?:und|oder)\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)?",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 10,
      "reasoning": "This rule captures the full entity including the title (e.g., 'Dr. Vogel') which was previously split or missed. The pattern ensures the title is optional but if present, it's part of the match. It uses a negative lookbehind to avoid matching titles that are part of a larger word."
    },
    {
      "name": "role_context_name",
      "description": "Matches person names appearing after specific legal role phrases (e.g., 'Senatspräsidenten', 'Hofrat') without requiring a title.",
      "format": "regex",
      "content": "(?:der\\s+Senatspr\\u00e4sident(?:in)?\\s+|der\\s+Vizepr\\u00e4sident(?:in)?\\s+|der\\s+Hofrat(?:in)?\\s+|der\\s+Hofr\\u00e4t(?:in)?\\s+|der\\s+Angeklagte(?:r)?\\s+|der\\s+Angeklagte(?:n)?\\s+|gegen\\s+|vertreten\\s+durch\\s+|als\\s+Vorsitzende(?:r)?\\s+)([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+(?:LL\\.M\\.|MBA|MSc|BSc|PhD)?)?)(?:\\s+(?:und|oder)\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)?",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 9,
      "reasoning": "This rule targets the specific context where names appear after legal roles. It captures the name part ($1) to avoid including the role text. It is more specific than the previous 'role_context_person' which was too broad and matched non-name words."
    },
    {
      "name": "sentence_start_name",
      "description": "Matches person names at the beginning of a sentence, but only if they are not common non-person capitalized words.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:^|[.!?]\\s+)([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+(?:LL\\.M\\.|MBA|MSc|BSc|PhD)?)?)(?:\\s+(?:und|oder)\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)?",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 8,
      "reasoning": "This is a refined version of 'sentence_start_person'. It captures the name ($1) to allow for better control. While still broad, it is necessary for cases like 'Sascha Aebel' at the start of a sentence. The priority is lower than title-based rules to allow more specific matches to take precedence."
    }
  ],
  "deleted_rules": [
    "sentence_start_person",
    "role_context_person",
    "title_only_person"
  ]
}

Description: Recognize named entities in German legal text. Entities to look for: person. German capitalizes all nouns, so rules must use strong context anchors 

Input schema: {'text': 'str'}
Output schema:
entities: List[Entity]

Entity:
  text: string  # The matched text span
  start: integer  # Start character offset
  end: integer  # End character offset
  type: string  # Entity label

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation

- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions
